extracted.intended_audience: Interested persons and stakeholders who submit petitions or comments to FMCSA, FMCSA staff and officials who implement Part 389 rulemaking procedures, and regulated entities (motor carriers, drivers) affected by FMCSA rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive requirements for initiating rulemakings, submitting comments and petitions, and for adoption and reconsideration of FMCSA rules under 49 CFR part 389 (including definitions and direct-final-rule procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Major rule — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Major rule means—(1) Any rule that the Administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs of the Office of Management and Budget finds has resulted in or is likely to result in: (i) An annual effect on the economy of $100,000,000 or more; (ii) A major increase in costs or prices for consumers, individual industries, geographic regions, or Federal, State, or local government agencies; or (iii) Significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or on the ability of United States-based enterprises to compete with foreign-based enterprises in domestic and export markets. (2) The term does not include any rule promulgated under the Telecommunications Act of 1996 and the amendments made by that Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FMCSA will adhere to the same guidance used under the Congressional Review Act and will interpret the term in consultation with OIRA, SBA, and DOT guidance; this definition is used to determine whether advanced participation (ANPRM or negotiated rulemaking) is required and to evaluate applicability of 49 CFR 5.17.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance public participation for potential major rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed rule regarding commercial motor vehicle safety is likely to lead to the promulgation of a major rule, the Administrator, before publishing such proposed rule, shall—(1) Issue an advance notice of proposed rulemaking that: (i) Identifies the need for a potential regulatory action; (ii) Identifies and requests public comment on the best available science or technical information relevant to analyzing potential regulatory alternatives; (iii) Requests public comment on the available data, benefits, and costs with respect to regulatory alternatives reasonably likely to be considered as part of the rulemaking; and (iv) Requests public comment on available alternatives to regulation; or (2) Proceed with a negotiated rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Administrator may waive paragraph (b) for good cause (incorporating a brief statement of reasons) when an ANPRM or negotiated rulemaking is impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest. Proposed rules subject to paragraph (b) should also be evaluated for applicability of 49 CFR 5.17 (DOT's economically significant/high-impact rule procedures). FMCSA added 'benefits' to clarify information desired in ANPRMs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition — definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Petition means a request for: (1) A new regulation; (i) A regulatory interpretation or clarification; or (ii) A determination made by the Administrator that a regulation should be modified or eliminated because it is: (A) No longer: (1) Consistent and clear; (2) Current with the operational realities of the motor carrier industry; or (3) Uniformly enforced; (B) Ineffective; or (C) Overly burdensome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory definition (FAST Act sec. 5204) frames what constitutes a petition for rulemaking; it may include requests to interpret or clarify existing rules and cannot omit the statutory elements (e.g., 'a regulatory interpretation or clarification'). FMCSA will provide transparency on petition status via its website and coordinate petition prioritization internally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written or in writing — permissible formats
rubrics_metrics.description: "Written or in writing" means printed, handwritten, typewritten either on paper or other tangible medium, or by any method of electronic documentation such as electronic mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition explicitly authorizes electronic submissions (including email and submissions via regulations.gov) as satisfying 'written' requirements; FMCSA added electronic submission options in §§389.31 and 389.35.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition submission content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Each petition filed under §389.31 must: (1) Be submitted in writing by mail to the Administrator or electronically at regulations.gov using the general petitions for rulemaking docket; (2) Set forth the text or substance of the rule or amendment proposed, or specify the rule that the petitioner seeks to have interpreted, clarified or withdrawn; (3) Explain the interest of the petitioner in the action requested; (4) Contain any information, data, research studies, and arguments available to the petitioner to support the action sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FMCSA removed duplicate-submission requirements and provided explicit procedures for electronic submissions. Petitioners should provide substantive evidence and arguments to aid FMCSA's evaluation; FMCSA may seek to provide additional public information on petitions and timelines in the future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of written comments — methods and language
rubrics_metrics.description: You may submit comments identified by the docket number using any of the following methods: (1) Federal eRulemaking Portal (regulations.gov); (2) Mail to Dockets Operations at DOT address; (3) Hand Delivery or Courier to Dockets Operations during business hours; (4) Fax. All written comments must be submitted in English and include copies of any material that the commenter refers to within the comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid duplication, use only one submission method. FMCSA declined to add regulatory text allowing submissions in languages other than English, but the Federal Register document soliciting comments can make exceptions. While incorporation by reference is not required for statutes/regulations (FMCSA can obtain copies), commenters are advised to quote or provide copies of other essential material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption and publication of final rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules are prepared by representatives from all relevant offices of FMCSA, submitted to the Administrator for consideration and forwarded, as necessary, to the Office of the Secretary for review and approval; once approved (and if necessary OMB/OIRA), the final rule is signed by the Administrator. All final rules must be published in the Federal Register unless all persons subject to the final rule are named and personally served with a copy of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FMCSA codified internal preparation and clearance procedures; although a rule is not legally binding until its effective date, FMCSA drafts final rules with intent to make them final. The process aligns with DOT's Administrative Rulemaking procedures at 49 CFR part 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitions for reconsideration — timing and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Any interested person may petition the Administrator for reconsideration of any rule issued under this part. The petition must be in English and submitted to the Administrator or electronically at regulations.gov, and received not later than thirty (30) days after publication of the rule in the Federal Register. Petitions filed after that time will be considered as petitions for rulemakings under §389.31. The petition must contain a brief statement of the complaint and an explanation as to why compliance with the rule is not practicable, is unreasonable, or is not in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FMCSA added electronic submission means for reconsideration petitions; late-filed petitions are treated as new rulemaking petitions under §389.31.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct final rule (DFR) / Notice of Intent (NOI) procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: If an individual intends to file an adverse comment, they may notify intent; under Departmental procedures, FMCSA will not be required to withdraw a DFR upon receipt of a notice of intent alone but will withdraw only upon actual receipt of an adverse comment. FMCSA may extend the comment period on a DFR at a request to allow time to file an adverse comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FMCSA declined to include prior NPRM changes to §389.39 in the final rule because the Department's December 2019 final rule revised direct final procedures across DOT. The practical effect: an NOI leads to extension consideration rather than automatic withdrawal; FMCSA will determine on a case-by-case basis whether to extend, withdraw, or proceed based on comments actually received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of waiver for advance rulemaking requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (b) of §389.13 (advance public participation requirements for potential major rules) does not apply if the Administrator, for good cause, finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons) that an advance notice of proposed rulemaking is impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waiver must be justified in the proposed or final rule with a brief statement of reasons. FMCSA retains discretion and will evaluate use of the waiver on a case-by-case basis; DOT procedures may only be waived per DOT-level authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information requested in ANPRMs — types of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: ANPRMs for potential major rules should identify the need for action and request public comment on the best available science or technical information, available data, benefits, and costs, and on available alternatives to regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FMCSA added 'benefits' to the regulatory text in response to comments; NYU and ACUS recommendations suggest FMCSA should explain what types of data and arguments are most useful, coordinate petition consideration with other priority processes, facilitate communication with petitioners, and invite public comment on petitions as appropriate—FMCSA indicates it has implemented many such recommendations and will provide additional transparency as it determines the best approach.
